t: Maximum Number That Makes Result of Bitwise AND Zero — Highest-Bit Observation
o: We need the largest x ≤ n such that x & (x+1) & … & n = 0. Claim: x = 2^b − 1 where b is the highest set bit of n. Why it works: the range contains 2^b (whose AND contribution is only bit b) and x (which has only bits below b), so the total AND is 0. Why it's maximal: any x′ > 2^b − 1 and ≤ n has bit b set, and 2^b itself lies in the range, forcing bit b into the AND — nonzero. All three examples match: 7→3, 9→7, 17→15. n ≤ 1e15 fits in 64-bit.
k: The power of two 2^b inside the range kills every candidate above 2^b − 1.

a.i: Take the bit length of n and return 2^(b−1) − 1.
a.t: O(1) — a single bit-scan (or O(log n) with the BigInt loop in JS)

a.i: Think greedily bit by bit: to maximize x while keeping the AND zero, set every bit below n's top bit and clear the top bit itself. Any attempt to keep the top bit fails because 2^b alone appears in the range. This derivation doubles as the proof of optimality.
s: Identify the highest bit b of n.
Set bits 0..b-1, clear bit b: x = 2^b − 1.
Verify: 2^b ∈ [x, n] forces AND = 0; anything larger keeps bit b via 2^b.

w: Tiny problem once the observation lands; spend interview time proving maximality rather than coding. Watch 64-bit handling in Java/C++ and use BigInt in JavaScript since n reaches 1e15 (still under 2^53, so Number would actually suffice, but BigInt is safer).
